title: How to start with AI? Professional solo dev
author: Necessary-Alps-5066
selftext:
Hello I am professional solo dev. My current process is as such:

1. Trusted contractors for art

2. Audio from assets

3. Make the game myself. Tech: either an engine or from scratch

  
Now I would like to start integrating AI into workflow. However its very challenging. I have no clue what are models, what is a prompt, etc. Right now my level is "Ask free ChatGPT something" and usually it gives me some disgusting LinkedIn answer and I have to correct it myself.

I did try to look through some projects and things here and sorry but I am not at the level to understand what is going on. Agents and prompts and all such things. Hopefully someone can explain just what is going on and how to use skilfully.

For my current game I will not use AI because I'm too deep in it. But after its release I am thinking of rebuilding my entire process. Any suggestions are welcome. Thank you in advance.

PS: I have 8GB 5060ti, I am also curious about local models and feasibility.

comments.author: Chocoweb88
comments.body:
Its quite interesting for me because I have absolutely zero knowledge and experience in both game coding and AI lol. So what I do is just tell AI my level and the game I want to make, then slowly chat with it to get mutual understanding and form a plan.

I use Claude Pro, first i ask this question:" I want to make XXX game with XXX engine. I have these assets or skills XXX, can guide me how to work with Claude (or whatever AI you use) to build this."

Then AI will explain the rest to you. Anything I dont undersatnd, I just ask AI to dumb it down and explain to me again.

Hope this can be helpful

comments.author: GedeonDar
comments.body:
Here is a quick way to start:  
\- get a 20$ ChatGPT Plus subscription   
\- install the Codex plugin on Visual Studio   
\- ask it to implement a small feature, system or tweak in your game

Some additional tips:  
\- create a Git branch first to isolate the changes and review them if you feel safer this way  
\- learn basics about Codex and LLM-assisted coding such as providing context, plan mode, models and thinking levels  
\- iterating in different strategies is the best way to find what AI usage makes more sense for you  
\- start with small requests, increase scope as you feel more confident   
\- I mention Codex but Claude works too, although the philosophy is slightly different

comments.author: Astra_Origin
comments.body:
simply subscribe to a provider. Since you already use ChatGPT free, sub to ChatGPT Plus and download the ChatGPT APP.   


  
\- The app acts as an IDE so to speak for agentic coding.   
\- Just add your project and you are ready to go (you can "optimize" [agents.md](http://agents.md) and download plugins, skills and mcp's as you go and need them)  
\- You already went down the correct path, dont ask random reddit users, asking your LLM will get you there faster.

comments.author: akanas
comments.body:
Don't even bother with local models. The difference between local model and frontier AI model is like a difference between amoeba and human. Those local models that could be somewhat comparable, would require 400GB of video memory, which is not local at all.

For unity AI usage there was a video tutorial from code monkey and other game developers provided videos how to use embedded unity AI.

For godot I just use Claude Code. Start fresh godot project, then open godot in claude code and task him to create a PoC. You can tell him from which dir to get assets. For 3d out of cilynders and squares it will create something instead, but from Synty Assets it was able to create quite interesting maps. Just write in plan English what you want.

comments.author: dossantosh
comments.body:
I’m a web developer where he use a lot of Claude code, not vibe coding but doc and automate solved problems

Actually right now I’m starting my first game project in godot(is text based so I think Claude will understand it more)

\- Use a repo for docs and code  
\- Create hooks, rules and skills, investigating what are those will be enough for you, you already are a profesional  
\- Try to make chats short (better inputs / outputs, avoids contamination, hallucination etc)  
\- Be very explicit, it’s a LLM not a human  
\- Have a “living” documentation. What I mean by this is make Claude manage docs, i think it will force you to document a lot, and have it updated because if not claude will tell you  
\- AI is really good as a investigation tool  
\- Another general advice is create a PR review in each push to a PR, that’s gonna be another Claude without chat context so it will help you askin questions about ideas / impl that the chat won’t get, to be it’s super useful

All this help me maintain better docs and code, but at the end of the day it’s up to you to get the ideas, the humanity in what you create, standard etc. 

You have more experience as a developer so you will know this better than me

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
Over 20 years of solo and professional development here. I only started using AI in May, but I wish I had this year's ago. 

Local models won't get you very far with 8Gb sadly. I was able to do some image generation and some image to 3d generation using my 3069 Ti and an 8Gb fork of Trellis2. Better than I expected, far short of commercial offerings. 

For coding agents though, it's just really not enough. You can use some models that offload to RAM but it slows thing down even further, and it will already be fairly slow even if you have a 16gb 5060, just because of the architecture (small memory bandwidth.)

For non local coding, I initially started off using VS Code and GitHub Copilot. I mainly used the inline suggestions for a while, but the chat interface drew my attention eventually.

You can describe what you're trying to do to it. Ask it to look at something that isn't working, and investigate why, even fix it for you. Or implement something - ones of the first things I had it do for me was implement a 3d galaxy map for my space game. When I saw how easily it did that and hooked it into current data sources, I decided to make my whole game 3d instead of the 2d I was initially making.

Don't underestimate the plan mode. It's how I do most things these days. A new game idea is first described with as much detail as I can, hitting all the main fun mechanics. A problem I need to fix is described in detail, with errors, screenshots, log dumps, whatever is useful pasted onto the chat. A new feature is described, even if it's just a vague idea, so that he AI can try to help me fill in the blanks. 

In plan mode the agent can ask you questions, generate all the roadmap and design documents, test the app or game itself (headless browser, headed browser, CDP), suggest alternatives, and estimate the amount of work. All before it starts making changes, so you can look at every step it wants to do and decide to make changes before anything happens. I think it's the most valuable part. 

Not all models are equal. I don't like Gemini for code, but it's good for working out ideas and pretty decent at concept artwork. GPT is great for code and images. You can even use it to edit images by text. The local models that will fit in 8Gb of VRAM are closer in capability to MiniGPT or Claude Haiku - not bad for small tasks or scripts, struggles with anything with decent context size. 

But I mainly use Claude Code. I'd been on Pro for the longest time, but I upgraded to Max last month. I use Claude Fable for planning, the hand off the documents to Claude Sonnet (easier tasks) and Claude Opus (harder tasks.) You can get pretty far with just Pro, and mixing which model you use. Opus for planning and Sonnet for implementing seems to work well. 

Good luck, I think it's an exciting time for developers.

comments.author: Professional_Ask3718
comments.body: The more context you can give it, the better it will perform, this goes for any time you use AI not just programming. Keep your tasks you ask it to do small, and if it is a larger request, ask it to break it up into smaller steps first and get it to tackle one at a time. I've found doing up a full design document, with all features that must be in the game and any that are desirable but not mandatory before you start is better. Even better since you have already done games in the past you could use these for context, even just giving it your coding style it can stick to the same conventions you normally do, provided it has that context first

comments.author: meathelix1
comments.body:
You would need a better GPU before you try local. 

I have 4 x 5090s and  4 x B70's, can run decent models well and so can just 1 5090. People who say local cant compete dont know how to setup local correctly. They are a total different game compared to just clicking a few buttons and connecting a MCP. 

Codex and even the cheap Chinese models will do you just fine.

comments.author: BJGG69
comments.body:
I'd recommend trying [combos.fun](http://combos.fun)  
  
Full disclosure: I am an affiliated creator there, but I have not been a game dev previously and do not have any coding knowledge, so I guess I needed a bit of a simpler starting experience, which combos offers. 

There is no separate setup or installation required, you just sign in and describe the request in a chat box. It works great for basic games and 2D, while more advanced 3D games require a lot more credits and time to build.   
  
May post a more in-depth experience sharing if there are enough people are interested.

comments.author: BansheeTheGame
comments.body: Try OpenCode as a low-pressure starting point; it has access to some free models. Use it on a real project for small tasks like implementing an isolated function or reviewing a diff. That should give you a practical sense of where even basic models help and where you still need to take over.

comments.author: MagnificentStumble_
comments.body:
Most of these comments are poor advice imo. I've been a web developer for the past 10 years, and heavily using AI to assist in development for the past 2 years or so, and now I barely even touch my IDE anymore.

I'm now successfully creating a game in Godot using AI with basically 0 prior knowledge about game development.

First, you want a paid subscription, free models aren't going to get you anywhere useful. Codex and Claude Code are the best. Arguably, Codex gets you the most bang for your buck, and it's what I use.

Below is my full setup. Open Codex Desktop, add your project's root directory, then set it to Sol 5.6 High and basically just paste the below list, and ask it to install everything for you, and if you want, ask it to explain what everything is and why to use it.

Here is my full setup:

\- IDE optimized for AI usage: [https://github.com/oraios/serena](https://github.com/oraios/serena)

\- Token usage optimization tool for LLMs: [https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk)

\- Full game development skillset for LLMs: [https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-game-dev-studio](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-game-dev-studio)

\- Allow LLMs to control and get context from Godot: [https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai](https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai) (replace this with whatever engine you use, all modern engines probably have an MCP server already)

Once everything is installed and configured, ask Codex to do the following for you:

\- Create an optimized [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) file for this project containing only the most important project context, design patterns and architecture. Do not repeat information that is already covered by skills.

That's it, you're basically set.

A few more tips I personally use:

\- Never ask the LLM to just start doing stuff, always ask it to make a plan first, and to persist that plan as a markdown file in the repository. I use Sol 5.6 High for creating all my plans.

\- Execute plans in a new chat context using Luna 5.6 High or better. This saves token usage and gets you the most out of your subscription.

\- When asking the LLM to execute a plan, explicitly mention that it should use the installed MCP server connection to test the implementation of the feature in-engine.

Any other questions you have, you should just ask ChatGPT or Codex. Once you move away from "asking questions in chatgpt" to granting Codex/Claude full access to your codebase, you basically improve your working speed by 100x.

comments.author: paulordbm
comments.body:
You can ask all of that to the AI itself. I'd recommend a cursor or Claude Code subscription. Cursor imho is very good and generous with your usage because their first party models are very good and among some of the best in the industry for cost effectiveness.

In summary: make sure you're using a good model like GPT Sol 5.6, Opus 5, Grok 4.6 or even Composer 2.5. look them up. Then, work on your prompts. Understand context is everything and the AI has none. It will need to gather context by looking at your code, looking on the web if you tell it to and from your own prompts. At the end of each session you manage a good output, ask the AI to improve your harness (AGENTS.md, skills, docs). These are multiple ways of "prompt injection", which means they're ways of adding content or context to your prompts so the AI knows what your game is, your goals, the way you prefer your code to be done, formatted, anything. It can contain important stuff, or frugal stuff. Context is everything, use every way possible to give enough of it to your agents.
